entry.title: University of Surrey Researcher Uses Mathematical Modelling to Personalize Sleep Predictions
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | surrey.ac.uk

Mathematical models of sleep regulation are being adapted to account for individual differences in sleep timing and brain activity cycles. By analyzing and restructuring the geometric components of existing sleep models, researchers can better simulate diverse sleep patterns, ranging from extreme night-owl tendencies to disrupted rapid eye movement cycles.

This research supports the development of digital calibration tools designed to help individuals predict how specific lifestyle modifications, such as morning light exposure, impact their rest. These personalized simulations aim to move beyond generic sleep advice and provide tailored strategies for improving sleep health.

entry.title: Connor Panter Study Examines Climate Change Impact on Britain’s Birds of Prey
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | frontiersin.org

New research by University of Nottingham researcher Connor Panter investigates how future climate change could alter environmental suitability for 16 breeding bird of prey species in the UK. Using computer models across various emissions scenarios, the study projects contrasting outcomes, with the peregrine falcon seeing potential habitat expansion while species like the short-eared owl, white-tailed eagle, red kite, and merlin face significant habitat reductions.

The author emphasizes that these models track shifting environmental conditions rather than guaranteed population movements or declines, as birds may adapt or face indirect pressures like changes in prey availability. Continued monitoring via citizen science platforms and mitigating existing threats such as illegal shooting are highlighted as vital components for long-term raptor conservation.

entry.title: Diseases Cured by AI Website Tracks Zero Approved Treatments
entry.content:
Links: diseasescuredbyai.com | hacker news

The tracking platform diseasescuredbyai.com reports that zero diseases have been cured by AI-discovered treatments as of November 2026, with no AI-designed drugs having yet received regulatory approval from the FDA or EMA. While billions of dollars flow into the AI drug-discovery market and over a hundred candidates have entered clinical trials, none have met the strict criteria of an AI-chosen target and molecule, regulatory approval, and a durable cure.

The database highlights candidates closest to breaking the zero threshold, including Insilico Medicine's rentosertib, which advanced to Phase III clinical trials for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and Takeda and Nimbus's zasocitinib, which faces an FDA review decision in early 2027. These developments represent advances in treatment and symptom management rather than complete cures, contrasting with optimistic timelines broadcast by industry executives predicting the elimination of major diseases within a decade.

entry.title: Study Shows Stone-Age Humans Needed Water and Workable Stone to Cross Arabia
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | nature.com

A new study reveals that early humans required both water and suitable stone for tool-making to inhabit and cross the Arabian Peninsula during the Middle Palaeolithic. While climate models indicate that ancient lakes and grasslands spread across the interior during humid phases, an expedition across the Rub’ al Khali desert found extensive lake deposits but a complete absence of stone tools or knappable rock.

Computer modeling of the entire peninsula demonstrates that 57% of terrain deemed habitable based on water alone lacked workable stone, shrinking the map of habitable land into fragmented zones. Because early toolmakers depended heavily on materials like chert and flint for daily survival, human dispersal across Arabia was constrained by geology as well as climate, stalling wherever the gaps between resource-rich areas became too wide to cross.

entry.title: Researchers Describe New Sauropodomorph Dinosaur Nyana rooiwalensis from South Africa
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | royalsocietypublishing.org

Palaeontologists have described a new species of early sauropodomorph dinosaur named Nyana rooiwalensis from Late Triassic rocks in South Africa's Eastern Cape. Unearthed in the Elliot Formation, the specimen includes an exceptionally well-preserved, near-complete skull from an individual that lived approximately 210 million years ago.

Although the animal weighed an estimated 400 kilograms, microscopic bone analysis indicates it was still a juvenile when it died, pointing to a rapid growth rate early in sauropodomorph evolution. The discovery provides critical anatomical details and new insights into how the ancestors of giant long-necked dinosaurs developed their massive body sizes.

Researchers surveyed 70 farmers across two villages to evaluate local breeding habits, finding that while participants prioritize traits like body size and twinning ability, they generally lack structured breeding programs.

The findings align with broader continental trends showing that unmanaged mating is widespread among African smallholder systems. Incorporating scientific selection metrics—such as evaluating rams for scrotal size and ewes for udder characteristics—alongside community-based breeding schemes could help enhance productivity while preserving locally adapted livestock traits.

The University of Waterloo provides documentation on the formalization of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis in Lean, following an initial release by Alpöge and Claude alongside a subsequent rewrite by Sernau and Anthropic. The original proof spans approximately 17 million lines across 175,187 files, while the compressed rewrite reduces the codebase to about 76,000 lines.

All 794 modules of the rewritten proof successfully compile, maintaining alignment with the original theorem statements. entry.title: Space Law Expert Analyzes Allegations of Russian Nuclear-Armed Satellite Threat
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Recent media reports citing NATO intelligence suggest that Russia could launch a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon into Earth's orbit as early as December. Such an action would directly violate Article IV of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which prohibits placing weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on celestial bodies.

While no country is known to have deployed a nuclear weapon in space, historical atmospheric tests like the United States' 1962 Starfish Prime demonstrated the severe electromagnetic and satellite damage such detonations cause. Experts note that verifying whether a satellite carries a nuclear payload remains technically challenging due to a lack of formal inspection procedures, though international dialogues continue to explore cooperative verification methods.

While high AI literacy correlates with an ability to recognize when they have been deceived, most people rely on intuition rather than proactive verification strategies like lateral reading. entry.title: New Study Reveals Fine-Scale Structure of New Zealand's Alpine Fault
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | science.org

Researchers used telecommunications fibre optic cables and distributed acoustic sensing to map New Zealand's 600-kilometre Alpine Fault in unprecedented detail. By recording seismic waves from nearby earthquakes, the team discovered that the fault is not a single crack but a 200-metre-wide band of damaged rock containing six narrower, intensely crushed cores about ten metres wide.

The findings show that one of these prominent cores extends continuously for about 180 kilometres underground, crossing a major change in the fault's surface geometry near Martyr River. Understanding whether a future rupture occurs on a single continuous surface or jumps between segments will help scientists model how seismic energy propagates and evaluate the magnitude and ground-shaking impacts of the next major earthquake.

entry.title: University of Oxford Researchers Use Seabird Audio Recorders to Track Unseen Vessels
entry.content:
Links: 404media.co | science.org

Researchers equipped northern gannets, Balearic shearwaters, and a Westland petrel with GPS devices and audio recorders to monitor their interactions with fishing vessels at sea. By comparing the recorded ship sounds with public tracking data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), the team evaluated how frequently seabirds encounter commercial ships across different oceans.

The study found that a significant percentage of the audio-detected vessel encounters—including about 32 percent for gannets in the North Atlantic and 12 percent for shearwaters in the Mediterranean—involved ships with their AIS trackers turned off. While the bio-logging method cannot determine whether trackers were disabled for illegal fishing or due to technical issues like poor satellite reception, researchers note that tracking bird-vessel interactions can improve bycatch risk assessments and illuminate hidden maritime activity.

Researchers analyzing nearly 40 years of data on over 450 wild Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Western Australia, have found that social predictability and consistent group sizes in old age are linked to greater longevity. Published in PLOS Biology, the study tracked how dolphins' social habits change throughout their lives, revealing patterns similar to human social ageing.

The findings indicate that while average dolphin group sizes increase and then decrease with age, individuals who maintain more predictable social behaviors live longer. The research highlights how stable social environments can buffer the effects of aging across long-lived species, providing new insights into the evolutionary roots of social aging.

entry.title: Mathematicians Adapt to AI-Generated Proofs by Focusing on "Digestion"
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

The rapid advancement of AI in mathematics—highlighted by a claimed 250,000-page solution to the generalized Riemann hypothesis by Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI's release of 722 AI-generated research papers—is forcing a fundamental shift in the field. While AI can now generate complex proofs and solutions that would take humans years to produce, these outputs are often incomprehensible to human researchers. The article argues that the core value of mathematics lies not just in reaching a solution, but in understanding the underlying logic and applying it to new contexts.

To preserve mathematical understanding, mathematicians are proposing a transition toward "digesting" proofs: absorbing, simplifying, and contextualizing AI-generated results to make them applicable. This shift may lead to significant changes in academia, including a move in Ph.D. programs to prioritize the explanation of solutions over their derivation and a shift toward oral exams in classrooms. Much like the calculator freed students from basic arithmetic, AI is expected to redefine mathematical research as a process of interpreting and applying technology-aided results.

entry.title: Meaning of Anthropic's Claimed VP ≠ VNP Proof
entry.content:
Links: friedgil.com | github.com | lobsters | hacker news

Anthropic recently published a paper authored by its Claude model claiming a proof that VP ≠ VNP. The distinction centers on the difference between the determinant and the permanent of a matrix: while the determinant can be computed in polynomial time using arithmetic circuits, the permanent is #P-complete and currently lacks a known polynomial-time algorithm. The claimed proof asserts that permanents cannot be computed using arithmetic circuits of polynomial size.

The separation of VP and VNP has significant implications for the P vs. NP problem. If P were to equal NP, any polynomial-time algorithm for computing permanents would have to rely on Boolean operators—such as AND, OR, and NOT—rather than the standard addition and multiplication operations used in arithmetic circuits. The proof suggests that such a "trick" would be necessary to bypass the limitations of arithmetic circuit complexity.

entry.title: University of Queensland Researchers Transmit Message Using Gravity
entry.content:
Links: news.uq.edu.au | science.org | lobsters | hacker news

University of Queensland researchers demonstrated a method of transmitting information using gravitational fields by moving a 1.8-tonne elevator counterweight. The team encoded binary data by shifting the counterweight's position, which was then detected by a sensitive gravimeter in an adjacent room through a brick wall. The experiment successfully transmitted the word "Gravity," proving that information can be encoded in and recovered from gravitational fields.

While current data rates are extremely low—yielding only one bit per minute—the study highlights the advantage of gravity's ability to bypass shielding that blocks standard electromagnetic signals, such as Wi-Fi or cellular data. Researchers suggest that the use of quantum sensors could eventually support data rates of 15 bits per minute over ranges of 500 meters, potentially enabling communication in environments where conventional signals cannot penetrate.

entry.title: Australian Ecologist Chris Dickman Dies
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Emeritus Professor Chris Dickman, a leading figure in Australian ecology and wildlife conservation, died on November 17, 2026. Known for his extensive research in the Simpson Desert and his work with the "ratcatchers" team, Dickman specialized in small marsupial populations and their roles in structuring ecological communities. He is widely recognized for co-leading the research that estimated three billion animals were impacted by Australia's 2019-20 bushfire crisis and for his early advocacy regarding dingo management and feral predator control.

Dickman’s career was marked by high-level leadership, including serving as president of the Australian Mammal Society and receiving the ESA Gold Medal. He was a highly regarded mentor who helped shape the careers of numerous ecologists and conservationists through his teaching and field leadership. In honor of his legacy, a celebratory forum and a festschrift—a collection of tributes from colleagues—were organized to commemorate his contributions to wildlife conservation and scientific communication.

entry.title: Wire-Fed Laser Steel Printing Proposed for Ageing Infrastructure Repair
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Ageing infrastructure in countries like the UK faces critical degradation under heavy operational demands, making the maintenance and life extension of existing steel structures an urgent necessity. Because traditional repair and replacement methods are highly disruptive and carbon-intensive, researchers are exploring advanced additive manufacturing techniques such as wire-fed laser-directed energy deposition to address structural wear.

This technique allows engineers to rebuild lost material precisely on deteriorated components using a laser beam and metal wire, potentially arresting fatigue cracks and restoring structural strength. Implementing such targeted repairs can significantly reduce carbon emissions, material consumption, and economic costs compared to complete structural replacements, though further research is required to ensure compatibility with legacy metal compositions.

entry.title: Evolutionary Origins of the First Animal on Earth
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Biologists have not identified the specific first animal to live on Earth, but they define animals as multi-celled organisms with specialized cells that communicate and share functions like movement, eating, and reproduction. Current research focuses on the deepest branches of the evolutionary tree, specifically debating whether sponges or comb jellies were the first to diverge from a common ancestor approximately 650 million years ago.

While fossils of soft-bodied early organisms are rarely preserved, genetic analysis of DNA architecture reveals how animals may have been "assembled" from existing single-celled "tool kits" found in relatives like choanoflagellates. By comparing these single-celled organisms to sponge choanocytes, scientists can better understand the transition from independent cells to the first coordinated multicellular life.

entry.title: Synthetic Allomelanin from Chernobyl Fungus Could Neutralize Nerve Agents
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | doi.org

Researchers have developed a material based on allomelanin, a nitrogen-free pigment produced by the radiation-resistant fungus Cladosporium sphaerospermum. By synthesizing allomelanin into nanoparticles and loading them with zirconium clusters, the team created a substance capable of trapping and chemically breaking down organophosphorus compounds, including deadly nerve agents like sarin and various agricultural pesticides.

Unlike current protective gear that merely traps toxins, this material employs "molecular scissors" to neutralize them, with reaction speeds significantly enhanced by sunlight and built-in alkaline groups. The study suggests these nanoparticles could be integrated into textiles to create proactive protective uniforms, gloves, and masks for soldiers and farmworkers facing chemical hazards.

entry.title: Phantom Decoy Technique Increases Wild Rat Trap Entry Rates, Study Shows
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | doi.org

Researchers investigating behavioural economics principles in wild black rats found that placing an unattainable, highly desirable food bait outside a tracking tunnel significantly increased entry rates. When a phantom decoy of peanut butter was positioned just out of reach at the entrance, rats were 83% more likely to enter tunnels containing basic food rewards compared to control setups.

Neophobia, or a natural caution around unfamiliar objects, frequently causes pest control trapping programs to fail when animals refuse to enter traps. The findings suggest that altering an animal's perceived options by introducing a decoy can effectively bypass this reluctance without requiring new trap designs or costly equipment.
